skills.title: CI
skills.summary: Pipelines that build and test every change, and keeping main green

concepts.title: Trunk-based development
concepts.summary: Merging small changes to the main branch at least daily, with unfinished work hidden behind flags

variants.q: A team's feature branches live for three weeks and merging them takes a day of conflict fixing. What does trunk-based development suggest instead?
choices: A long-lived `develop` branch that every feature merges into first
Merge small changes into main daily, behind flags
Freeze main during the last week of each sprint for stabilisation
Rebase every feature branch onto main once a week
variants.explain: Integrating small changes often keeps divergence, and so conflicts, small. A `develop` branch just moves the big merge somewhere else.

variants.q: In trunk-based development, how do you merge part of a feature that isn't ready for users yet?
choices: Keep it on a branch until the whole feature is finished
Merge it into a release branch only, never into main
Merge it behind a flag that's off in production
Merge it to main, then revert it before each deploy
variants.explain: Flags let incomplete code ship to main and even to production without being reachable by users. Keeping it on a branch is exactly the long-lived divergence trunk-based development avoids.

concepts.title: Build once, promote the artifact
concepts.summary: Building one image or binary and deploying that same artifact to every environment

variants.q: A pipeline rebuilds the Docker image from the same commit for staging and again for production. Staging passed, but production behaves differently. What practice prevents this class of problem?
choices: Promote one image digest through every environment
Add a longer soak period in staging before production
Use exactly the same Dockerfile for both of the builds
Tag both images with the commit SHA they were built from
variants.explain: Two builds of one commit can pull different base images or dependency versions, so what you tested isn't what you ship. Promoting a single digest guarantees it is; tagging two builds with the same SHA just hides the difference.

variants.q: If the same artifact is deployed to staging and production, where do the differences between environments (database URL, API keys) come from?
choices: Separate build flags compiled into each environment's artifact
Config injected at deploy or run time
A different branch of the repo for each environment
A config file baked into the image, edited after deploy
variants.explain: Keeping config outside the artifact is what makes one artifact deployable everywhere. Baking per-environment values in means rebuilding per environment, which defeats the point.

concepts.title: Pinning CI actions to a commit SHA
concepts.summary: Referencing third-party CI actions by full commit hash, because tags can be moved

variants.q: A workflow uses `uses: some-org/some-action@v3`. Why do security guides recommend `@<full commit SHA>` instead?
choices: Pinning to a SHA makes the workflow start up faster
Version tags are deprecated in GitHub Actions workflows
Tags can be moved to new code; a full SHA can't
GitHub caches actions only when they're pinned by SHA
variants.explain: Git tags are mutable, so whoever controls the action's repo can point `v3` at new, possibly malicious, code that your CI runs with your secrets. A full commit SHA always refers to the same content.

variants.q: An attacker takes over a popular CI action's repository and re-points all its version tags at code that prints secrets to the log. Which workflows keep running the old, safe code?
choices: Those using a full commit SHA
Those using a major tag like `@v2`
Those using an exact tag like `@v2.4.1`
Those using the `@main` branch
variants.explain: Any tag, however specific, can be force-moved. Only a full commit SHA is immutable, which is why it's the recommended pin for third-party actions.

concepts.title: Merge queue
concepts.summary: Testing each PR combined with main and the PRs ahead of it before merging, so main stays green

variants.q: PR A renames a function. PR B, opened earlier, adds a new call to the old name. Both pass CI on their own and both merge. Main is now broken. What prevents this?
choices: Requiring two approving reviews on every PR
Re-running CI on every open PR each night
Squash-merging instead of creating merge commits
A merge queue that tests the combined result
variants.explain: Each PR was tested against an older main, so nobody tested the combination. A merge queue builds and tests the actual result of merging before it lands.

variants.q: Why does a busy repo use a merge queue instead of just requiring "branch must be up to date with main" before merging?
choices: Up-to-date branches can't run CI until they're merged
It does the rebase-and-retest loop for everyone
Merge queues skip CI entirely for small, low-risk PRs
Merge queues let PRs merge without waiting for review
variants.explain: Requiring up-to-date branches gives the same safety, but every merge invalidates all other PRs and starts a rebase race. A queue tests the combined state for you, often batching PRs together.

concepts.title: CI cache keys
concepts.summary: Keying dependency caches on a hash of the lockfile so the cache updates when dependencies change

variants.q: A GitHub Actions cache step uses the fixed key `deps-cache`. Months later, builds still restore very old dependencies and reinstall most packages. Why?
choices: Caches expire after 24 hours and are rebuilt from scratch
Restoring a cache always clears it for the next run
An exact key hit isn't saved again, so it never updates
Fixed keys are shared across every repo in the org
variants.explain: `actions/cache` doesn't overwrite an existing key, so a constant key freezes the first snapshot. Including `hashFiles('**/package-lock.json')` in the key creates a new cache whenever dependencies change.

variants.q: Why include a hash of the lockfile (`go.sum`, `package-lock.json`, `uv.lock`) in a CI dependency cache key?
choices: A new entry is made whenever dependencies change
It makes the cache encrypted at rest on the runner
It lets the same cache be shared with production builds
Every run becomes a cache hit, even after an upgrade
variants.explain: The key changes exactly when the dependency set changes, so you get hits on unchanged builds and fresh entries after an upgrade. A fallback `restore-keys` prefix can still start from the nearest older cache.

skills.title: Release & deployment
skills.summary: How code reaches production, rollouts and rolling back

concepts.title: Blue-green deployment
concepts.summary: Running the new version beside the old one and switching all traffic over at once

variants.q: In a blue-green deployment, the new version (green) is live and errors spike. What is the fastest rollback?
choices: Rebuild the previous version and redeploy it
Restart green's pods in case that clears the errors
Switch traffic back to blue
Roll forward with a hotfix
variants.explain: Blue is kept running and unchanged, so rollback is a traffic switch that takes seconds. Rebuilding or hotfixing takes minutes to hours while users see errors.

variants.q: Blue and green share one database. The green release includes a migration. What must be true of that migration for blue-green rollback to stay safe?
choices: It must run only after blue has been deleted
Blue must still work with the new schema
It must target a separate database for green
Nothing: blue-green isolates the database itself
variants.explain: Rolling back sends traffic to blue, which now runs against the migrated schema. If the migration dropped or renamed something blue uses, the rollback fails.

concepts.title: Canary release
concepts.summary: Sending a small share of traffic to the new version and widening it only if metrics stay healthy

variants.q: A new version gets 5% of traffic. Its error rate is 3% while the old version's is 0.2%. What does a canary process do next?
choices: Increase to 25% to get a bigger sample
Keep 5% running and file a bug
Move everyone to the new version, since 95% of users weren't affected
Stop the rollout and send all traffic back to the old version
variants.explain: The point of a canary is to compare the new version with the baseline on real traffic and abort when it is worse. Widening a clearly bad canary turns a small incident into a big one.

variants.q: What makes a canary release more than "deploying slowly"?
choices: Gating each step on canary vs baseline metrics
Deploying to one region at a time, in a fixed order
Running the canary only at night when traffic is low
Requiring manual approval before each pod restarts
variants.explain: Without measuring the canary against the baseline, a gradual rollout just spreads a bad release more slowly. The health comparison and automatic abort are what catch problems early.

concepts.title: Feature flags
concepts.summary: Shipping code switched off and turning it on separately, decoupling deploy from release

variants.q: A new checkout flow is deployed to production behind a flag that's off, then enabled for 1% of users a week later. What does this separate?
choices: Building the code from testing it
Deploying code from releasing it
Staging from production
Code review from merging
variants.explain: The deploy moved code to production; the flag decides who sees it. That lets you release (and un-release) without a deploy.

variants.q: A feature behind a flag causes problems for the 10% of users who have it. What is the quickest fix?
choices: Revert the commit and redeploy
Restart the pods
Turn the flag off
Scale the service up
variants.explain: A flag acts as a kill switch: switching it off takes effect without a build or deploy. Reverting works too, but takes a full pipeline run.

concepts.title: Version skew during rolling deploys
concepts.summary: Old and new versions run side by side during a rollout, so each must handle the other's data and calls

variants.q: A rolling deploy replaces pods one at a time over ten minutes. The new version stops writing a field that the old version requires when reading. What happens during the rollout?
choices: Nothing: old pods are drained before any new pod starts
The deploy tool blocks the rollout automatically
Only new pods see errors
Old pods can fail on records written by new pods
variants.explain: During a rolling update both versions serve traffic and share data. Changes have to be backward and forward compatible for that window, which is why removals are done in a later release.

variants.q: You want to rename a message field consumed by another service. Producers and consumers deploy independently. Which plan avoids breaking either side?
choices: Rename it in both services in one PR and deploy them together
Write both names, move readers, then drop the old one
Rename it in the producer first; consumers fail until they update
Version the topic name and delete the old topic the same day
variants.explain: Independent deploys can't be made simultaneous, so there is always a window with mixed versions. Writing both fields covers that window; the old one is removed only after every reader has moved.

concepts.title: Graceful shutdown
concepts.summary: On SIGTERM: refuse new requests, let in-flight ones complete, release connections, then exit

choices: `Shutdown` can't be called from a different goroutine
`ListenAndServe` ignores `Shutdown` and keeps serving
`log.Fatal` exits before in-flight requests drain
`context.Background()` makes `Shutdown` return at once
variants.explain: `ListenAndServe` returns right away once `Shutdown` is called; the program must then wait for `Shutdown` itself to return. Treat `ErrServerClosed` as expected and block until draining is done.

variants.q: A Kubernetes pod gets SIGTERM and its process exits within 50 ms. For a few seconds afterwards, some clients still get connection errors. What is the usual fix?
choices: Keep serving a few seconds after SIGTERM, then drain
Exit even faster so the pod is replaced sooner
Increase the liveness probe's timeout and period
Raise the number of replicas so the gap is covered
variants.explain: Endpoint removal runs concurrently with SIGTERM, and load balancers and kube-proxy on every node take a moment to drop the pod. A short pause before closing (in the app, or a `preStop` sleep) lets those stragglers be served.

variants.q: A rolling deploy ends a pod while it is halfway through a 20-second report export, and the client gets a connection reset. The pod's termination grace period is 30 seconds. What should the app do on SIGTERM?
choices: Ignore SIGTERM and keep running until Kubernetes sends SIGKILL
Finish only the requests that are under one second long
Stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests, then exit
Exit immediately, since the client will retry the export
variants.explain: Draining means refusing new requests while in-flight ones complete within the grace period. Exiting at once drops the export, and ignoring SIGTERM means the work ends abruptly at SIGKILL anyway.

skills.title: Docker
skills.summary: Writing Dockerfiles and building and running containers

concepts.title: Layer cache ordering
concepts.summary: Copying dependency manifests and installing before copying source, so code edits don't reinstall everything

variants.q:
Every one-line code change makes this build reinstall all dependencies. Why?

```dockerfile
FROM node:22
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```
choices: `npm ci` always ignores the Docker layer cache
`WORKDIR` resets the layer cache on every build
The `node:22` base image tag isn't pinned to a digest
`COPY . .` changes with any file, so `npm ci` reruns
variants.explain: A layer is rebuilt when its inputs change, and so is everything after it. Copying `package.json` and the lockfile first, running `npm ci`, then copying the rest keeps the install layer cached until dependencies change.

variants.q: Which ordering keeps the dependency download cached across code-only changes in a Go image?
choices: Copy all, download modules, build
Copy `go.mod`/`go.sum`, download modules, copy all, build
Download modules, copy all, build
Copy all, copy `go.mod`/`go.sum`, download modules, build
variants.explain: Copying only the module files before downloading makes that layer depend on dependencies alone. Copying everything first, even if the module files are copied again, means any code edit invalidates the download layer; downloading before any copy fails because there's no `go.mod` yet.

concepts.title: Multi-stage builds
concepts.summary: Building in one stage and copying only the output into a small runtime image

variants.q: A Dockerfile builds in a `FROM golang` stage and then has `FROM gcr.io/distroless/static` with `COPY --from=build /out/app /app`. What ends up in the final image?
choices: The binary on a minimal base, no toolchain or source
Both stages, with the build stage hidden from `docker run`
The source code and the binary, but not the compiler
Only the build stage, since it appears first in the file
variants.explain: Only the last stage becomes the image, and it contains just what was copied into it. The compiler, source and build cache stay in the discarded build stage.

variants.q: Why are multi-stage builds a security improvement, not just a size one?
choices: They encrypt the final image's layers at rest
They scan the image for known CVEs during the build
Compilers and build tools aren't shipped
They run the whole build without any network access
variants.explain: Each package left out of the runtime image is one less thing with vulnerabilities or useful to an attacker who gets in. Scanning is a separate step that multi-stage builds don't perform.

concepts.title: PID 1 and signals
concepts.summary: A container's PID 1 gets no default signal actions, so it must handle SIGTERM itself or pass it on

variants.q: A container's main process runs as PID 1 and installs no handler for SIGTERM. You run `docker stop`. What happens?
choices: The process exits immediately, as with any SIGTERM
Docker falls back to sending SIGINT, which it handles
The process is restarted inside the same container
It's ignored, then SIGKILLed after the grace period
variants.explain: The kernel doesn't apply default signal actions to PID 1 of a PID namespace, so an unhandled SIGTERM does nothing. Handle SIGTERM in the app or run under a small init such as `tini` (`docker run --init`).

variants.q:
The image uses `ENTRYPOINT ["/app/start.sh"]`, and the script is:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
./migrate
node server.js
echo "server exited"
```

On `docker stop`, why doesn't the Node server shut down gracefully?
choices: Node can't receive signals when running inside a container
The shell is PID 1 and doesn't forward SIGTERM to `node`
The `echo` line runs first and closes the server's socket
Exec-form `ENTRYPOINT` blocks every signal to the script
variants.explain: Signals go to PID 1, here the shell, and `sh` doesn't pass them on to the child it is waiting for. Launching the server with `exec node server.js` makes Node PID 1, and Node then needs its own SIGTERM handler (or an init like `tini` in front) to shut down cleanly.

concepts.title: Secrets in image layers
concepts.summary: Files deleted in a later layer and build args stay readable in the image; use build secrets instead

variants.q:
Is the token still recoverable from the final image?

```dockerfile
COPY .npmrc /root/.npmrc
RUN npm ci
RUN rm /root/.npmrc
```
choices: No: the `rm` step removes it from the image
No: only the last layer's files are kept on push
Yes: the `COPY` layer still holds the file
Only to someone with a shell in a running container
variants.explain: Each instruction adds a layer, and a later `rm` only hides the file in the merged view. Use a BuildKit secret mount (`RUN --mount=type=secret,...`) so the file never lands in a layer.

variants.q: A Dockerfile has `ARG NPM_TOKEN` and uses it in a `RUN` step. Why is this unsafe for a secret?
choices: Build args can't be read by `RUN` steps
Its value is recorded in the image's history
Build args are uploaded to the registry's logs
`ARG` values are set in the running container
variants.explain: Docker warns that build args are visible in `docker history` and in max-mode provenance attestations. `ARG` values aren't set in the running container's environment (that's `ENV`); use `RUN --mount=type=secret` instead.

concepts.title: .dockerignore
concepts.summary: Excluding files like `.git`, `.env` and local `node_modules` from the build context

variants.q: A repo has no `.dockerignore` and the Dockerfile does `COPY . .`. Which of these is the most serious consequence?
choices: A local `.env` with real credentials lands in the image
The build can no longer use the layer cache for any step
The `Dockerfile` itself gets copied into the final image
Docker refuses to build without a `.dockerignore` file
variants.explain: Without exclusions the whole directory, secrets included, becomes part of the context and the image. Slower builds and larger images are side effects; a leaked credential is the real damage.

variants.q: A Node image builds fine on CI but crashes on a Mac developer's local build with an error from a native module. The Dockerfile runs `npm ci` and later `COPY . .`. What is the likely cause?
choices: `npm ci` doesn't support native modules in containers
The base image was pulled for the wrong CPU architecture
`COPY . .` brings the host's macOS `node_modules`
Docker Desktop disables native modules on macOS hosts
variants.explain: Without `node_modules` in `.dockerignore`, the host's install overwrites the one built for Linux in the image. CI has no local `node_modules`, so it doesn't happen there.

skills.title: Environment management
skills.summary: Config and secrets across dev, staging and production

concepts.title: Config in the environment
concepts.summary: Keeping per-environment settings out of the code and supplying them at run time (Twelve-Factor)

variants.q: A codebase has `config.staging.json` and `config.prod.json` committed, with database URLs and passwords. What does the Twelve-Factor approach recommend instead?
choices: Encrypt the two files and keep them in the repo
Build a separate artifact for each environment
Move the files to a dedicated `config/` branch
Set them per environment at deploy time
variants.explain: Config that differs per deploy belongs outside the code, so one artifact runs anywhere and secrets never live in the repo. Separate artifacts per environment break the build-once rule.

variants.q: Which value is "config" in the Twelve-Factor sense, and so should come from the environment?
choices: The payment provider's API base URL
The list of HTTP routes this service exposes to callers
The JSON schema of the service's request bodies
The names of the tables in the service's database
variants.explain: Config is whatever varies between deploys (a sandbox URL in staging, the live one in production). Routes, request schemas and table names are part of the code and are the same everywhere.

concepts.title: Validating config at startup
concepts.summary: Parsing and checking every setting when the process starts, so bad config crashes the deploy, not a request

variants.q:
`HTTP_TIMEOUT` is not set in production. What does the client do?

```go
d, _ := time.ParseDuration(os.Getenv("HTTP_TIMEOUT"))
client := &http.Client{Timeout: d}
```
choices: It falls back to Go's default 30-second client timeout
It panics with a parse error on the first request
No timeout at all: `d` is zero
It fails to compile because there's no default value
variants.explain: `os.Getenv` returns `""` for unset variables, parsing fails, and the zero `Duration` means no timeout on `http.Client`. Validate settings at startup and refuse to boot on a missing or invalid one.

choices: `maxRetries` is `NaN`, and `0 < NaN` is false
`maxRetries` is `0`, because `Number(undefined)` is `0`
`maxRetries` is `null`, and `0 < null` is false
`maxRetries` is `undefined`, and `0 < undefined` is false
variants.explain: `Number(undefined)` is `NaN` (it's `Number(null)` and `Number("")` that give `0`), and every comparison with `NaN` is false, so the loop silently never runs. Parse env vars with a schema at startup so this fails loudly instead.

variants.q: Which line makes a missing `DATABASE_URL` stop the service as soon as it starts?
choices: `URL = os.getenv("DATABASE_URL")` at module level
`URL = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]` at module level
`os.environ.get("DATABASE_URL")` inside the first query
`os.getenv("DATABASE_URL", "")` inside the pool setup
variants.explain: Indexing `os.environ` raises `KeyError` for a missing key, and at module level that happens at import, before the service accepts traffic. `getenv` returns `None` (or the default), so the failure turns up later, on a request.

variants.q: A service reads `PAYMENT_API_URL` lazily on the first checkout and falls back to an empty string if it is unset. A deploy to production misses the variable. When does anyone find out?
choices: At deploy time, because the rollout health check fails
At startup, because every runtime refuses to boot with empty values
Never: the empty string is replaced by a sensible default
On the first customer checkout, and only if someone sees the error
variants.explain: Lazy reads with a silent default push the failure to the first request that needs the value. Validating all required settings at startup makes the bad deploy fail its health check before taking traffic.

concepts.title: Configuration drift
concepts.summary: Real infrastructure diverging from what's in code, usually through manual changes

variants.q: During an incident someone edits a Terraform-managed security group in the cloud console to open an extra port. What happens on the next `terraform apply` from the unchanged code?
choices: Terraform imports the manual change into the code automatically
Terraform skips resources that were edited by hand
The apply fails until the console change is reverted
The plan shows drift and the apply reverts it
variants.explain: Terraform reconciles real resources toward the code, so a manual change shows up as drift and gets undone. Fixes made by hand need to go back into code, or they disappear.

variants.q: Staging and production were built from the same scripts a year ago, but a bug now appears only in production. Investigation finds a different kernel parameter on prod hosts that nobody remembers setting. What is this an example of?
choices: Version skew
Configuration drift
Cache poisoning
Bit rot
variants.explain: Environments that started the same diverge through untracked manual changes. Defining infrastructure as code and regularly detecting drift keeps them comparable.

concepts.title: Rotating a leaked secret
concepts.summary: Once a secret is committed or exposed, revoke and replace it; deleting it from the code isn't enough

variants.q: An API key was committed and pushed to a shared repo. A follow-up commit removes it. What still needs to happen?
choices: Nothing more: the key is no longer in the code
Squash the two commits so the key disappears from history
Make the repo private so nobody else can see the commit
Revoke the key and issue a new one
variants.explain: Git history, forks, clones and CI logs keep the old value, and automated scanners pick up pushed keys quickly. Rotation is the only real fix; rewriting history is cleanup on top.

variants.q: A database password was printed in a CI log visible to the whole company. The log was deleted within an hour. What is the right next step?
choices: Rotate it and check for use during the exposure
Nothing, since the log was deleted within the hour
Restrict who can read CI logs from now on, to prevent repeats
Change the port the database listens on
variants.explain: You can't know who read or copied it in that hour, so treat it as compromised. Restricting log access is a good follow-up but doesn't fix this exposure.

concepts.title: Preview environments
concepts.summary: A short-lived, full copy of the app deployed per pull request and torn down when it merges

variants.q: Five teams share one staging environment, and someone's half-finished change often blocks everyone's testing. What addresses this directly?
choices: A second staging environment for the team that breaks it most
A shared booking calendar for the staging environment
A preview environment per PR, deleted on merge
Testing only in production, behind feature flags
variants.explain: Per-PR environments isolate each change, so one broken branch no longer blocks the others. A calendar or extra fixed environment just rations the contention.

variants.q: A team wants a preview environment for every PR. What has to be true first?
choices: Every PR must be reviewed and signed off by QA first
Setup and teardown are fully automated
The app must be able to run as a single container
Production data must be copied into each preview
variants.explain: Environments created per PR only work if setup and teardown are scripted end to end. Copying production data is usually something to avoid, for privacy reasons.

skills.title: Cloud
skills.summary: Using cloud services (compute, storage, IAM) and running workloads on them

concepts.title: Least privilege
concepts.summary: Giving each service and person only the permissions it needs, scoped to the resources it uses

variants.q: A service only reads objects from one bucket. Its role has `storage:*` on all buckets "to be safe". What is the main risk?
choices: Requests get slower when a role has broad permissions
A compromise exposes every bucket
The cloud provider bills extra for wildcard permissions
The service is more likely to be rate limited
variants.explain: Permissions set the blast radius of a compromise. Read-only on the one bucket limits damage to what the service needed anyway.

variants.q: Which policy follows least privilege for a worker that writes results to `reports/` in one bucket?
choices: Admin on the project, restricted by network rules
Write access to every bucket in the account
Read and write on the whole bucket
Write only, on `reports/` in that bucket
variants.explain: The narrowest action set on the narrowest resource is least privilege. Network rules don't limit what a compromised process with admin rights can do.

concepts.title: Kubernetes requests and limits
concepts.summary: Requests reserve capacity for scheduling; going over the CPU limit throttles, over the memory limit kills

variants.q: A container regularly goes over its memory limit. What does Kubernetes do?
choices: Throttles the container until its usage drops
Moves the pod to a node with more free memory
Kills it (OOMKilled, exit 137)
Logs a warning and lets the container continue
variants.explain: Memory can't be throttled the way CPU time can, so the kernel's OOM killer ends the process and the app gets no chance to log why. Throttling is what happens at the CPU limit, not the memory limit.

variants.q: An API's latency spikes under load and health checks start timing out, but the pod never restarts for memory. Usage graphs show it pinned at its CPU limit. What is happening?
choices: It's CPU-throttled, so all work runs slower
It's being OOMKilled silently and restarted
The scheduler keeps moving it between nodes
Its CPU request is set too high for the node
variants.explain: Going over a CPU limit doesn't kill anything; the kernel restricts how much CPU time the container gets, so work slows down. Raise the limit or scale out.

concepts.title: Runtime heap vs container memory limit
concepts.summary: Telling the language runtime about the container's memory limit so its GC works before the OOM killer does

variants.q: A Go service has about 600 MiB of live heap, a 1 GiB container limit, default `GOGC=100` and no `GOMEMLIMIT`. It gets OOMKilled at traffic peaks. Which change addresses this most directly (Go 1.19+)?
choices: Set `GOMAXPROCS` to match the container's CPU limit
Set `GOGC=200` so collections happen less often
Call `runtime.GC()` on a timer every few seconds
Set `GOMEMLIMIT` a bit under the limit
variants.explain: With `GOGC=100` the heap can grow to about twice the live heap before the next GC, past 1 GiB here. `GOMEMLIMIT` makes the GC work harder as total memory nears the limit; raising `GOGC` makes it worse.

variants.q: A Node service runs in a 1 GiB container with `--max-old-space-size=4096`. Under load memory climbs. How does it most likely die?
choices: OOMKilled by the kernel (exit 137), no JS stack
A JS `heap out of memory` error at the 4 GiB heap cap
The event loop blocks and the liveness probe restarts it
V8 shrinks the heap to fit the container automatically
variants.explain: The flag tells V8 it may grow the heap to 4 GiB, so it lets garbage pile up past what the container allows and the kernel kills the process. Set the old-space size below the container limit; about three quarters of it is a common rule of thumb, leaving room for buffers and native memory.

variants.q: A service on a garbage-collected runtime holds about 600 MiB of live data in a 1 GiB container. It is OOMKilled at peak traffic, even though live data fits. What is the underlying cause and fix?
choices: Live data is leaking; the only fix is to find and remove the leak
The runtime lets the heap grow past the container limit; set a heap ceiling below it
The container's CPU limit is too low for the collector; raise it
The garbage collector never runs in containers; trigger it manually
variants.explain: A runtime sizes its heap from its own settings or the host, not the container's cgroup limit, so garbage can pile up until the kernel kills the process. A leak is possible but not implied: live data stayed at 600 MiB.

variants.q: A Java service in a 1 GiB container is started with a maximum heap of 1 GiB, and it is still OOMKilled while the heap shows no out-of-memory error. Why?
choices: Heap memory is not counted against the container limit until a full GC
Kubernetes always kills pods whose heap is above 80% of the limit
Thread stacks, metaspace and native buffers count toward the limit too
The container limit applies only to the memory the heap has already used
variants.explain: The container limit covers the whole process, not just the heap, so a heap ceiling equal to the limit leaves no room for stacks, metaspace and native memory. The heap itself counts as it grows, so the kill can come before the runtime ever reports its own out-of-memory error.

concepts.title: Liveness vs readiness probes
concepts.summary: Readiness decides if a pod gets traffic; liveness decides if it is restarted, and shouldn't check dependencies

variants.q: The liveness probe of every API pod checks that the database answers. The database has a 30-second blip. What happens?
choices: Pods stop getting traffic until the database is back
All pods fail liveness and restart together
Kubernetes fails over to a replica database automatically
Nothing, since liveness ignores failures under a minute
variants.explain: Liveness failures trigger restarts, and a restarted pod finds the same unreachable database, so every pod churns at once and then reconnects together. Liveness should check only the process itself; dependency trouble is at most a readiness concern.

variants.q: A pod is still loading a large cache at startup and shouldn't get requests yet, but it isn't broken. Which probe should report failure?
choices: Liveness
Both liveness and readiness
Readiness
Neither: Kubernetes waits for the container to start
variants.explain: Readiness keeps traffic away without killing the pod (a startup probe can also hold off liveness during a slow boot). Failing liveness here would restart the pod before it ever finishes loading.

concepts.title: Choosing the autoscaling signal
concepts.summary: Scaling on the metric that tracks this workload's load, such as queue depth for a worker

variants.q: A queue consumer spends most of its time waiting on an external API. CPU stays at 15% while the backlog grows to millions of messages. It autoscales on CPU. What should it scale on?
choices: Memory usage
Queue backlog or consumer lag
Number of HTTP requests to the pod
Node CPU instead of pod CPU
variants.explain: For an I/O-bound consumer, CPU doesn't reflect how far behind it is. Backlog (or lag, or oldest message age) measures the work waiting, which is what scaling should respond to.

variants.q: Scaling out a consumer from 10 to 50 replicas doesn't reduce the backlog, and the downstream database's connections are now maxed out. What is the lesson?
choices: Scale to 100 replicas so the backlog finally drops
Switch the autoscaler's signal from CPU to memory
Make the consumers retry failed writes faster
Cap replicas at what the downstream can take
variants.explain: When the limit is downstream, more consumers just add load where it hurts. Set a maximum based on what the dependency can handle and fix the real bottleneck.

skills.title: Observability
skills.summary: Logs, metrics, traces and alerts: knowing if a system is healthy

concepts.title: Structured logging
concepts.summary: Logging events as key-value fields (usually JSON) so they can be filtered and searched

variants.q:
What does this `log/slog` call log for the trailing `"user"` argument?

```go
slog.Info("login failed", "user")
```
choices: `user=` with an empty value
A compile error, because the arguments are unbalanced
Nothing: the extra argument is dropped
`!BADKEY=user`, since a key has no value
variants.explain: slog takes alternating keys and values; a lone string at the end has no value, so it is logged as a value under the key `!BADKEY`. `go vet` (Go 1.21+) flags the mismatched pair, and `slog.String("user", id)` avoids it.

variants.q:
With `logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)`, what shows up for this call?

```python
log.info("order created", extra={"order_id": oid})
```
choices: The message, with `order_id` as a JSON field
Only the message: `extra` isn't in the format
An error, because `extra` needs a custom formatter
`order_id` appended to the message as `key=value`
variants.explain: `extra` attaches attributes to the log record, but the default format string only includes the level, logger name and message. You need a JSON formatter (or a format string naming the field) for it to be emitted.

variants.q: Why log `{"msg": "payment failed", "invoice_id": "inv_7", "provider": "x"}` instead of the string `"payment failed for invoice inv_7 via x"`?
choices: The JSON line takes fewer bytes to store
Log shippers drop lines that aren't JSON
You can query by field, not by regex
String logs can't safely include IDs
variants.explain: Structured fields let a log tool query "all failures for provider x" directly. With free text you depend on regexes that break whenever the wording changes.

variants.q: Service A logs `{"userId": 7}`, service B logs `{"user_id": 7}` and service C logs `{"uid": 7}`. An engineer wants every log line for user 7 across the three services. What is the problem?
choices: The numeric value 7 should have been logged as a string
Each service needs its own log aggregation pipeline
One query can't match all three, because field names differ
JSON logs can't be searched across services
variants.explain: Structured logs only pay off when field names are consistent, since queries are by field. Agreeing on a shared schema (or normalising at ingest) lets one query find the user everywhere.

concepts.title: Trace context propagation
concepts.summary: Passing the trace ID across every hop (the `traceparent` header, message metadata) so one request is one trace

variants.q: Service A calls service B over HTTP and both are instrumented with OpenTelemetry. How does B know its spans belong to A's trace?
choices: B queries A's tracing backend by timestamp to match spans
A sends a `traceparent` header that B continues
Both services share a global trace ID set at deploy time
The load balancer matches spans up by client IP address
variants.explain: Trace context travels with the request; each service reads it, creates child spans, and passes it on. Without propagation, B starts a new, unrelated trace.

variants.q: HTTP traces look complete, but every trace stops where service A publishes to a queue, and the consumer's work shows up as separate traces. What is missing?
choices: The consumer's trace sampling rate is set too low
The broker has to be restarted with tracing switched on
The consumer must use the same service name as A
The context isn't put in the message headers
variants.explain: Async hops have no HTTP header, so the producer must put the context in message metadata and the consumer must extract it. Many queue client libraries need instrumentation for this to happen.

concepts.title: Latency percentiles
concepts.summary: Using p50/p95/p99 instead of averages, which hide the slow requests users notice

variants.q: An endpoint's average latency is 90 ms and its p99 is 3.2 s. What does that mean?
choices: The endpoint is fast; the p99 is noise
Most requests take around 3.2 s
About 1 request in 100 takes 3.2 s or longer
The average is wrong and should be recomputed
variants.explain: p99 is the value 99% of requests are under, so 1% are at or above it. Averages blend that tail into fast requests and hide it.

variants.q: A page makes 20 backend calls in parallel and must wait for all of them. Each call's p99 is 1 s. Why is a single call's p99 a poor guide to the page's speed?
choices: Parallel calls are always slower than sequential ones
One slow call in 20 delays the whole page
p99 only applies to single-threaded code paths
The page's latency is the average of the 20 calls
variants.explain: With 20 independent calls, the chance at least one is in its slowest 1% is about 18%. Fan-out makes tail latency the common case, so look at the tail end to end.

concepts.title: Aggregating latency with histograms
concepts.summary: Percentiles can't be averaged across instances; combine histograms, then compute the percentile

variants.q: Each of 10 pods reports its own p99 latency. A dashboard shows the average of those ten numbers as "service p99". What is wrong?
choices: An average of percentiles isn't a percentile
It should be the sum of the ten values instead
Nothing, as long as every pod gets equal traffic
It should be the median of the ten values instead
variants.explain: The true p99 depends on the whole distribution, which the ten summaries have thrown away. Exporting histograms (bucket counts) lets you add buckets across pods and compute the real percentile.

variants.q: Why do Prometheus users usually record request latency as a histogram rather than a summary when they want a service-wide p99?
choices: Histograms use less memory than summaries in every case
Summaries can't record latency values, only counts
Histogram buckets can be summed across pods
Summaries are only available in the Go client
variants.explain: A summary's quantiles are computed per instance and can't be combined; histogram bucket counters can be added up and fed to `histogram_quantile`. The price is that the percentile is an estimate limited by bucket boundaries.

concepts.title: Metric label cardinality
concepts.summary: Each unique label combination is a separate time series, so unbounded labels blow up the metrics store

variants.q: Someone adds a `user_id` label to `http_requests_total`. The service has 2 million users. What is the likely effect?
choices: Nothing: labels are just text attached to one series
Queries get more precise, with no other cost
The client library rejects labels with over 100 values
Millions of new series, overloading the backend
variants.explain: Every distinct label value creates its own series. Per-user detail belongs in logs or traces; metric labels should come from small, bounded sets like status code or route.

variants.q: Which label is safe on a request-count metric?
choices: The raw URL path, such as `/orders/98213`
The route template, such as `/orders/:id`
The request ID
The client's IP address
variants.explain: A route template has a small, fixed set of values. Raw paths, request IDs and IPs are unbounded and each creates new series.

concepts.title: RED and USE methods
concepts.summary: RED (rate, errors, duration) for services; USE (utilization, saturation, errors) for resources

variants.q: You are building a first dashboard for an HTTP service. Which three signals does the RED method say to show?
choices: Rate, errors, duration
Replicas, events, deploys
Utilization, saturation, errors
Retries, exceptions, downtime
variants.explain: RED describes a service from its callers' view: how much traffic, how much fails, how slow. Utilization, saturation and errors is USE, which is for resources like CPU, disks and pools.

variants.q: Using the USE method on a database connection pool, which measurement is "saturation"?
choices: The share of pool connections currently in use
The number of failed connection attempts
Requests waiting for a free connection
The average query duration on the pool
variants.explain: Saturation is work that can't be served yet and is queued. Share in use is utilization; failed attempts are errors.

skills.title: Incident response
skills.summary: Handling incidents: mitigating, escalating and learning afterwards

concepts.title: Mitigate first, root cause later
concepts.summary: Stopping user impact (rollback, flag off, failover) before working out exactly why it happened

variants.q: Error rates jumped right after a deploy 10 minutes ago. Nobody knows the cause yet. What should happen first?
choices: Read the diff until the bug is found, then hotfix
Roll back the deploy, then investigate
Add more logging and redeploy to learn more
Wait to see whether it recovers on its own
variants.explain: The deploy is the obvious suspect and rolling back is quick and low-risk, so it ends user impact now. Finding the root cause can happen calmly afterwards; debugging live keeps users waiting.

variants.q: During an incident one engineer wants to keep debugging a promising theory, while another can fail over to a healthy region in two minutes. What does good incident practice favour?
choices: Debug first, since failing over destroys evidence
Run both at once without telling each other
Wait until the incident commander joins
Fail over now, keeping logs for later
variants.explain: Restoring service comes before understanding it, as long as you capture what you need for the review. The faulty region can still be investigated after traffic has moved.

concepts.title: Alerting on symptoms
concepts.summary: Paging on user-visible impact such as error rate or latency, not on internal causes like CPU

variants.q: Which alert is most worth waking someone up for?
choices: Login 5xx rate above 1% for 10 minutes
CPU above 90% on any pod in the cluster
Disk usage at 60% on the shared log volume
A pod restarted once in the last hour
variants.explain: A symptom alert fires when users are actually affected and points at what to fix. High CPU can be perfectly healthy, so paging on it wakes people for nothing and trains them to ignore pages.

variants.q: An on-call engineer gets 40 pages a week and most need no action. What is the right response?
choices: Add more on-call engineers to share the pages
Lower thresholds so real problems are caught sooner
Tune or remove the alerts nobody acts on
Forward all alerts to a chat channel nobody owns
variants.explain: Alert fatigue makes people miss the page that matters. Every page should mean a human needs to act now; the rest go to tickets or dashboards.

concepts.title: SLOs and error budgets
concepts.summary: A reliability target over a window, and the amount of failure it allows before reliability work takes priority

variants.q: An SLO says 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days. If the service were fully down, roughly how much downtime would use the whole error budget?
choices: About 4.3 minutes
About 7.2 hours
About 43 minutes
About 3.6 days
variants.explain: 0.1% of 30 days (43,200 minutes) is about 43 minutes. 4.3 minutes would be a 99.99% target.

variants.q: A team has used its whole error budget for the month with two weeks left. Under a typical error budget policy, what changes?
choices: The SLO target is lowered for the rest of the month
Risky launches pause; reliability work comes first
Nothing changes until the next month starts
The team stops all deploys, including bug fixes
variants.explain: The budget is the agreed trade-off between shipping and reliability; once spent, the balance tips toward reliability. Fixes that improve reliability still ship, so a total freeze isn't the point.

concepts.title: Burn-rate alerting
concepts.summary: Alerting on how fast the error budget is being spent, over a short and a long window

variants.q: With a 30-day SLO window, a burn rate of 1 means the budget will be exactly used up in 30 days. Sustained for 1 hour, what share of the 30-day budget does a burn rate of 14.4 use?
choices: About 14%
About 0.5%
About 48%
About 2%
variants.explain: One hour is 1/720 of 30 days, so 14.4 × 1/720 = 2% of the budget. That's why a high burn rate over a short window is a common paging threshold.

variants.q: Why do burn-rate alerts often require both a long window (say 1 hour) and a short window (say 5 minutes) to be over the threshold?
choices: Long window shows it's real; short shows it's ongoing
Most monitoring tools can't evaluate a single-window rule
The short window catches problems the long one never sees
It halves the number of alert rules that need maintaining
variants.explain: A long window alone keeps firing for a while after the problem is fixed; a short window alone is noisy. Requiring both gives alerts that are significant and current.

concepts.title: Incident commander
concepts.summary: One person who coordinates the response and makes calls, rather than debugging hands-on

variants.q: In a major incident, what is the incident commander's main job?
choices: Find and fix the root cause personally
Write the postmortem while the incident runs
Coordinate roles, decisions and updates
Approve every command before anyone runs it
variants.explain: The commander keeps the response organised so responders can focus on the system. If they dive into debugging, nobody is watching the whole picture.

variants.q: Eight engineers have joined an incident call, three are trying different fixes at the same time, and nobody is updating stakeholders. What is the most useful first move?
choices: Ask everyone to keep trying fixes until one works
Name a commander who assigns roles
Remove everyone except the most senior engineer
Start writing the postmortem timeline right away
variants.explain: Uncoordinated changes make it impossible to tell what helped or hurt. A clear commander and roles turn a crowd into a response.

concepts.title: Running a blameless postmortem
concepts.summary: Reviewing an incident to find how the system allowed it and what to change, without blaming individuals
